title: Memories of Louis, the Mexican dance bands and local fame at Sherman
summary: Chicago and Armstrong memories kept him in jazz; Mexican bands from Chino and Corona hired him for dances while he was at school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You know, ever since then -- I think it was the memories of, of that -- I . . .

Yes, memories of Chicago and Louis Armstrong that kept me in jazz. And I . . . begin my own improvisations, and I, I would -- whenever in the trombone, I begin to think of jazz a little -- more in a directly, so to speak, I, I, I wanted, wanted to be a jazz musician in the worst way possible, even then when I was goin' to school. And when I went to school there, there used to be some Mexican bands around Chino, California and Corona, California. And they would come and pick me up to play at the dances. And in that way, I used to make my little bread, my money outside of school. And I was pretty well known as the jazz coming up, up and coming jazz man of the year.

"The jazz trombonist" of Riverside, California. So, you really began to attract some attention there then. That's remarkable. Were there any other of your fellow students who may have been musically inclined who tried to play with you, or that you were able to play with, or any people in the vicinity?
There wasn't anybody here that at that time that was interested in jazz, but I think it's because they just didn't have the a, the background that I had and have
